title: Quadratic Functions & Equations
description: Standard, vertex, and factored forms; completing the square; quadratic formula; discriminant; Vieta's formulas; inequalities; optimisation.

notes.heading: Forms of a Quadratic
notes.body:
A quadratic function is any function of the form $f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$ where $a 
eq 0$. Its graph is a parabola. The way you write the equation reveals different features instantly.

📌 Standard Form
    $$f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$$
• The y-intercept is $(0, c)$ — just substitute $x = 0$.
• The axis of symmetry is $x = - rac{b}{2a}$.
• The vertex has x-coordinate $- rac{b}{2a}$.

📌 Vertex Form
    $$f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k$$
• The vertex is at the point $(h, k)$.
• The axis of symmetry is $x = h$.
• If $a > 0$, the parabola opens upward (∪ shape) and the vertex is a minimum.
• If $a < 0$, the parabola opens downward (∩ shape) and the vertex is a maximum.

📌 Factored Form
    $$f(x) = a(x - p)(x - q)$$
• The x-intercepts (roots) are at $x = p$ and $x = q$.
• The axis of symmetry is exactly halfway between the roots: $x =  rac{p + q}{2}$.
• Substitute $x = 0$ to find the y-intercept: $f(0) = apq$.

💡 Worked Example — Finding the Vertex from Standard Form
Find the vertex of $f(x) = 2x^2 - 8x + 1$.

  Step 1: Identify $a$ and $b$
    $a = 2$,  $b = -8$

  Step 2: Find the axis of symmetry
    $$x = - rac{b}{2a} = - rac{(-8)}{2 	imes 2} =  rac{8}{4} = 2$$

  Step 3: Find the y-coordinate of the vertex
    $$f(2) = 2(2)^2 - 8(2) + 1 = 8 - 16 + 1 = -7$$

  Answer: The vertex is $(2, -7)$.

💡 Worked Example — Converting Factored to Standard Form
Find the y-intercept of $f(x) = -3(x - 2)(x + 5)$.

  Step 1: Expand the brackets
    $$f(x) = -3(x^2 + 5x - 2x - 10) = -3(x^2 + 3x - 10)$$

  Step 2: Distribute the $-3$
    $$f(x) = -3x^2 - 9x + 30$$

  Answer: The y-intercept is $30$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $a$ controls width and direction: $|a| > 1$ → narrower; $|a| < 1$ → wider.
• The three forms are equivalent — you can always expand or factorise to switch between them.
• Vertex form is best for graphing; factored form is best for finding roots.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Mixing up the sign in vertex form. In $f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k$, the vertex is $(h, k)$, NOT $(-h, k)$. For example, $f(x) = 3(x + 2)^2 - 5$ has vertex $(-2, -5)$.

notes.heading: Solving Quadratics
notes.body:
There are three main ways to solve a quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$: factorising, completing the square, and the quadratic formula. Each has its own best-use case.

📌 Method 1: Factorising (Null Factor Law)
If you can write $ax^2 + bx + c$ as a product of two linear factors, then:
    $$(px + q)(rx + s) = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad px + q = 0 	ext{ or } rx + s = 0$$
This is the fastest method when the quadratic factors neatly.

📌 Method 2: Completing the Square
Rewrite $ax^2 + bx + c$ in the form $a(x + h)^2 + k$.
When $a = 1$:
    $$x^2 + bx + c = \left(x +  rac{b}{2}ight)^2 -  rac{b^2}{4} + c$$
When $a 
eq 1$, factor $a$ out from the $x$-terms first.

📌 Method 3: The Quadratic Formula
For any quadratic $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ with $a 
eq 0$:
    $$x =  rac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$$

🔑 The Discriminant
The expression under the square root is called the discriminant:
    $$\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$$
• $\Delta > 0$  →  two distinct real roots
• $\Delta = 0$  →  one repeated real root (the parabola touches the x-axis)
• $\Delta < 0$  →  no real roots (the parabola does not cross the x-axis)

💡 Worked Example — Using the Quadratic Formula
Solve $2x^2 - 5x - 3 = 0$.

  Step 1: Identify $a$, $b$, $c$
    $a = 2$,  $b = -5$,  $c = -3$

  Step 2: Calculate the discriminant
    $$\Delta = (-5)^2 - 4(2)(-3) = 25 + 24 = 49$$

  Step 3: Apply the formula
    $$x =  rac{5 \pm \sqrt{49}}{4} =  rac{5 \pm 7}{4}$$

  Step 4: Find both solutions
    $$x =  rac{5 + 7}{4} =  rac{12}{4} = 3$$
    $$x =  rac{5 - 7}{4} = - rac{2}{4} = - rac{1}{2}$$

  Answer: $x = 3$  or  $x = - rac{1}{2}$

💡 Worked Example — Completing the Square
Write $x^2 + 6x + 5$ in the form $(x + h)^2 + k$.

  Step 1: Take half the coefficient of $x$ and square it
    $$\left( rac{6}{2}ight)^2 = 9$$

  Step 2: Add and subtract this value inside the expression
    $$x^2 + 6x + 5 = (x^2 + 6x + 9) + 5 - 9$$

  Step 3: Factor the perfect square
    $$= (x + 3)^2 - 4$$

  Answer: $(x + 3)^2 - 4$, so the vertex is $(-3, -4)$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always try factorising first — it is the quickest method when it works.
• Completing the square is essential for deriving the quadratic formula and for graphing.
• The quadratic formula always works, even when factorising is difficult.
• If a quadratic has no real roots, you can still find complex roots using the same formula.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Dividing both sides of an equation by $x$. For example, solving $x^2 = 5x$ by dividing by $x$ gives $x = 5$ and loses the solution $x = 0$. Always rearrange to make the RHS zero before factorising.

notes.heading: Vieta's Formulas
notes.body:
When a quadratic equation has roots, there is a beautiful relationship between the coefficients and the roots — even if you never find the roots explicitly.

📌 Definition
For the quadratic $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ with roots $\alpha$ and $ eta$:
    $$	ext{Sum of roots:} \quad \alpha +  eta = - rac{b}{a}$$
    $$	ext{Product of roots:} \quad \alpha eta =  rac{c}{a}$$

These are called Vieta's formulas (or the sum-and-product of roots).

🔑 Why They Matter
• Check your answers: if you solve a quadratic, the sum and product of your solutions should match $- rac{b}{a}$ and $ rac{c}{a}$.
• Form a quadratic from its roots: if roots are $\alpha$ and $ eta$, the monic quadratic is $x^2 - (\alpha +  eta)x + \alpha eta = 0$.
• Solve problems without finding roots: many symmetric expressions in $\alpha$ and $ eta$ can be evaluated directly.

💡 Worked Example — Forming a Quadratic from Roots
Find a quadratic equation with roots $2$ and $-5$.

  Step 1: Find the sum and product
    $	ext{Sum} = 2 + (-5) = -3$
    $	ext{Product} = 2 	imes (-5) = -10$

  Step 2: Write the monic quadratic
    $$x^2 - (	ext{sum})x + (	ext{product}) = 0$$
    $$x^2 - (-3)x + (-10) = 0$$

  Step 3: Simplify
    $$x^2 + 3x - 10 = 0$$

  Answer: $x^2 + 3x - 10 = 0$

💡 Worked Example — Evaluating without Finding Roots
If $\alpha$ and $ eta$ are roots of $2x^2 - 7x + 3 = 0$, find $\alpha^2 +  eta^2$.

  Step 1: Use Vieta's formulas
    $$\alpha +  eta =  rac{-(-7)}{2} =  rac{7}{2}$$
    $$\alpha eta =  rac{3}{2}$$

  Step 2: Rewrite $\alpha^2 +  eta^2$ using the identity
    $$\alpha^2 +  eta^2 = (\alpha +  eta)^2 - 2\alpha eta$$

  Step 3: Substitute
    $$= \left( rac{7}{2}ight)^2 - 2\left( rac{3}{2}ight)$$
    $$=  rac{49}{4} - 3$$
    $$=  rac{49}{4} -  rac{12}{4}$$
    $$=  rac{37}{4}$$

  Answer: $\alpha^2 +  eta^2 =  rac{37}{4}$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Vieta's formulas work for any quadratic, even when the roots are complex.
• For a monic quadratic ($a = 1$), the formulas simplify to: sum = $-b$, product = $c$.
• Common symmetric expressions: $\alpha^2 +  eta^2 = (\alpha +  eta)^2 - 2\alpha eta$ and $ rac{1}{\alpha} +  rac{1}{ eta} =  rac{\alpha +  eta}{\alpha eta}$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting the minus sign in the sum formula. The sum of roots equals $- rac{b}{a}$, not $ rac{b}{a}$. If the quadratic is $x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0$, the sum of roots is $5$ (not $-5$) because $- rac{b}{a} = - rac{(-5)}{1} = 5$.

notes.heading: Inequalities and Optimisation
notes.body:
Quadratic inequalities and optimisation problems appear constantly in IB exams. The key is understanding how the parabola shape determines where the expression is positive or negative.

📌 Solving Quadratic Inequalities
To solve $ax^2 + bx + c > 0$ (or $< 0$, $\geq 0$, $\leq 0$):

  1. Find the roots by solving $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$.
  2. Sketch the parabola using the sign of $a$.
  3. Read the solution from the graph.

🔑 The Sign Rule
• If $a > 0$ (parabola opens upward):
    $$ax^2 + bx + c > 0 \quad ightarrow \quad 	ext{outside the roots } (x < 	ext{smaller root} 	ext{ or } x > 	ext{larger root})$$
    $$ax^2 + bx + c < 0 \quad ightarrow \quad 	ext{between the roots}$$
• If $a < 0$ (parabola opens downward), the inequalities reverse.

📌 Optimisation with Quadratics
For $f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$, the vertex gives the extreme value:
• If $a > 0$, the minimum value occurs at $x = - rac{b}{2a}$.
• If $a < 0$, the maximum value occurs at $x = - rac{b}{2a}$.

💡 Worked Example — Quadratic Inequality
Solve $x^2 - x - 12 < 0$.

  Step 1: Find the roots
    $$x^2 - x - 12 = 0$$
    $$(x - 4)(x + 3) = 0$$
    $$x = 4 	ext{ or } x = -3$$

  Step 2: Determine the shape
    $a = 1 > 0$, so the parabola opens upward.

  Step 3: Read the solution
    We want where the parabola is below the x-axis — between the roots.

  Answer: $-3 < x < 4$

💡 Worked Example — Optimisation
A ball is thrown upward and its height after $t$ seconds is $h(t) = -5t^2 + 20t + 1$ metres. Find the maximum height and when it occurs.

  Step 1: Identify $a$ and $b$
    $a = -5$,  $b = 20$

  Step 2: Find the time at the vertex
    $$t = - rac{b}{2a} = - rac{20}{2 	imes -5} = - rac{20}{-10} = 2 	ext{ seconds}$$

  Step 3: Find the maximum height
    $$h(2) = -5(2)^2 + 20(2) + 1 = -20 + 40 + 1 = 21 	ext{ metres}$$

  Answer: Maximum height is $21$ m at $t = 2$ s.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always make the RHS zero before solving an inequality.
• When multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, flip the inequality sign.
• For optimisation, always check that your answer makes sense in the real-world context (e.g., time cannot be negative).
• The vertex formula $x = - rac{b}{2a}$ is faster than completing the square for finding maxima/minima.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing the solution to $x^2 - x - 12 > 0$ as $x < -3$ and $x > 4$ (using "and" instead of "or"). These are two separate intervals that do not overlap, so the correct connective is "or". In interval notation: $(-\infty, -3) \cup (4, \infty)$.

notes.heading: Positive and Negative Definite Quadratics
notes.body:
Some quadratics are always positive or always negative — they never cross the x-axis. Recognising these quickly saves time and prevents sign errors.

📌 Definitions
• A quadratic is positive definite when $ax^2 + bx + c > 0$ for ALL real $x$.
• A quadratic is negative definite when $ax^2 + bx + c < 0$ for ALL real $x$.

🔑 Test for Definiteness
    $$	ext{Positive definite} \iff a > 0 	ext{ AND } \Delta < 0$$
    $$	ext{Negative definite} \iff a < 0 	ext{ AND } \Delta < 0$$

Why does this work? The discriminant $\Delta < 0$ means there are no real roots, so the parabola never touches the x-axis. The sign of $a$ then tells you whether the entire graph is above ($a > 0$) or below ($a < 0$) the x-axis.

💡 Worked Example — Testing for Positive Definite
Show that $x^2 + 2x + 3$ is positive definite.

  Step 1: Check the coefficient of $x^2$
    $$a = 1 > 0 \quad ightarrow \quad 	ext{parabola opens upward}$$

  Step 2: Calculate the discriminant
    $$\Delta = b^2 - 4ac = (2)^2 - 4(1)(3) = 4 - 12 = -8$$

  Step 3: Apply the test
    $$a > 0 	ext{ and } \Delta < 0 \quad ightarrow \quad 	ext{positive definite}$$

  Answer: $x^2 + 2x + 3 > 0$ for all real $x$.

💡 Worked Example — Finding a Parameter for Definiteness
For what values of $k$ is $x^2 - 4x + k$ positive definite?

  Step 1: Identify $a$, $b$, $c$
    $a = 1$,  $b = -4$,  $c = k$

  Step 2: Apply the positive definite condition
    Need $a > 0$ (true, since $a = 1$) AND $\Delta < 0$

  Step 3: Solve $\Delta < 0$
    $$\Delta = (-4)^2 - 4(1)(k) = 16 - 4k$$
    $$16 - 4k < 0$$
    $$16 < 4k$$
    $$k > 4$$

  Answer: The quadratic is positive definite when $k > 4$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The phrase "definite" means the quadratic has a definite sign — it never changes.
• If $\Delta \geq 0$, the quadratic is neither positive nor negative definite (it crosses or touches the x-axis).
• Positive definite quadratics are useful for proving inequalities and showing expressions are always positive.
• Negative definite quadratics are less common but appear in certain optimisation and proof problems.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Checking only $\Delta < 0$ without checking the sign of $a$. A quadratic with $a < 0$ and $\Delta < 0$ is negative definite, not positive definite. Both conditions must be verified.

notes.heading: Line and Parabola Intersection
notes.body:
Finding where a straight line meets a parabola is a classic IB problem. The number of intersection points is controlled by the discriminant of the combined equation.

📌 Definition
To find where the line $y = mx + c$ meets the parabola $y = ax^2 + bx + d$, set the equations equal:
    $$ax^2 + bx + d = mx + c$$
Rearrange into standard quadratic form and solve.

🔑 How it works
• Two distinct solutions  →  the line cuts the parabola in two places.
• One repeated solution  →  the line is tangent to the parabola.
• No real solutions  →  the line misses the parabola entirely.

The discriminant of the resulting quadratic tells you which case applies.

💡 Worked Example — Finding Intersection Points
Find where the line $y = 2x + 3$ meets the parabola $y = x^2$.

  Step 1: Set the equations equal
    $$x^2 = 2x + 3$$

  Step 2: Rearrange to standard form
    $$x^2 - 2x - 3 = 0$$

  Step 3: Factorise
    $$(x - 3)(x + 1) = 0$$

  Step 4: Find y-coordinates
    When $x = 3$: $y = 2(3) + 3 = 9$
    When $x = -1$: $y = 2(-1) + 3 = 1$

  Answer: $(3, 9)$ and $(-1, 1)$

💡 Worked Example — Tangency Condition
Find the value of $c$ so that $y = 2x + c$ is tangent to $y = x^2 + 3x + 1$.

  Step 1: Set equal
    $$x^2 + 3x + 1 = 2x + c$$

  Step 2: Rearrange
    $$x^2 + x + (1 - c) = 0$$

  Step 3: Apply tangency condition $\Delta = 0$
    $$\Delta = 1^2 - 4(1)(1 - c) = 1 - 4 + 4c = 4c - 3$$

  Step 4: Solve
    $$4c - 3 = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad c =  rac{3}{4}$$

  Answer: $c =  rac{3}{4}$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always rearrange to $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ before calculating $\Delta$.
• Tangency means the line touches the parabola at exactly one point.
• The combined equation can sometimes factorise; if not, use the quadratic formula.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting to find the y-coordinate after solving for $x$. An intersection point needs both coordinates.

notes.heading: Modelling with Quadratics
notes.body:
Quadratic functions model many real-world situations: projectiles, areas, profit, and bridge shapes. The key skill is translating words into an equation, then using the vertex or roots to answer the question.

📌 Definition
A quadratic model has the form $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ where the independent variable $x$ represents time, length, price, or another quantity, and $y$ represents height, area, profit, or another output.

🔑 Key Concept
In applications the vertex usually gives the maximum or minimum value of the model, while the roots tell you when the output is zero. Always check whether the mathematical answer makes sense in the real-world context.

💡 Worked Example — Maximising Area
A farmer has $60$ m of fencing to make a rectangular enclosure against a straight wall. Find the maximum possible area.

  Step 1: Define variables
    Let the side perpendicular to the wall be $x$ m. Then the side parallel to the wall is $(60 - 2x)$ m.

  Step 2: Write the area model
    $$A(x) = x(60 - 2x) = 60x - 2x^2$$

  Step 3: Find the vertex
    $$x = - rac{b}{2a} = - rac{60}{2(-2)} = 15 	ext{ m}$$

  Step 4: Find the maximum area
    $$A(15) = 15(60 - 30) = 15 	imes 30 = 450 	ext{ m}^2$$

  Answer: The maximum area is $450 	ext{ m}^2$.

💡 Worked Example — Projectile Motion
A stone is thrown from a height of $2$ m. Its height is $h(t) = -5t^2 + 12t + 2$. When does it hit the ground?

  Step 1: Set height to zero
    $$-5t^2 + 12t + 2 = 0$$

  Step 2: Use the quadratic formula
    $$t =  rac{-12 \pm \sqrt{12^2 - 4(-5)(2)}}{2(-5)} =  rac{-12 \pm \sqrt{144 + 40}}{-10}$$
    $$t =  rac{-12 \pm \sqrt{184}}{-10}$$

  Step 3: Take the positive root
    $$t \approx  rac{-12 + 13.56}{-10} \approx -0.16 	ext{ (reject)}$$
    $$t \approx  rac{-12 - 13.56}{-10} \approx 2.56 	ext{ s}$$

  Answer: The stone hits the ground after approximately $2.56$ seconds.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Identify which quantity you are maximising or minimising before choosing a method.
• Reject answers that are negative or outside the practical domain.
• Round final answers to a sensible number of significant figures.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using the x-coordinate of the vertex as the final answer when the question asks for the maximum value. Always substitute back to find the actual output.

flashcards.definition: Rewrite $ax^2+bx+c$ as $a(x+h)^2+k$ to reveal the vertex and solve.
The vertical line through the vertex: $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$.
$y=a(x-h)^2+k$: vertical stretch by $|a|$, reflection if $a<0$, shift $h$ right, shift $k$ up.

flashcards.term: Tangency of a line and parabola
flashcards.definition: A line is tangent to a parabola when setting them equal gives a quadratic with $\Delta=0$.
flashcards.example: $y=x+c$ is tangent to $y=x^2$ when $x^2-x-c=0$ has $\Delta=1+4c=0$, so $c=-\frac{1}{4}$.

flashcards.definition: For $a>0$, $ax^2+bx+c>0$ outside the roots and $<0$ between the roots; reverse if $a<0$.

questions.explanation: Factorising gives $(x-2)(x-3)=0$, so the solutions are $x=2$ or $x=3$.

questions.stem: Which condition guarantees that $ax^2+bx+c$ is positive for all real $x$?
questions.explanation: The parabola must open upward ($a>0$) AND never touch the x-axis ($\Delta<0$). Together these make the quadratic positive definite.

questions.stem: By completing the square, write $2x^2-8x+5$ in the form $a(x-h)^2+k$.
A ball is thrown upward. Its height after $t$ seconds is $h(t)=-4t^2+16t+3$ metres. What is the maximum height reached?
questions.explanation: The maximum occurs at $t=-\frac{b}{2a}=-\frac{16}{-8}=2$ s. Substituting: $h(2)=-4(4)+16(2)+3=-16+32+3=19$ m.

questions.stem: A quadratic has roots $3$ and $-2$, and its y-intercept is $-12$. Find its equation.
For what values of $k$ is $x^2-4x+k$ positive for all real $x$?
questions.explanation: Need $\Delta<0$. $\Delta=(-4)^2-4(1)(k)=16-4k<0 \rightarrow 4k>16 \rightarrow k>4$. When $k>4$, the parabola opens upward and never touches the x-axis, so it is always positive.

questions.stem: The line $y=3x+c$ is tangent to the parabola $y=x^2+5x+2$. Find $c$.
questions.explanation: Set equal: $x^2+5x+2=3x+c \rightarrow x^2+2x+(2-c)=0$. For tangency, $\Delta=0$. $\Delta=4-4(2-c)=4c-4=0 \rightarrow c=1$.

questions.stem: The graph of $y=x^2$ is transformed by a vertical stretch of factor $2$, then a translation of $\binom{3}{-1}$. What is the equation of the image?
questions.explanation: Vertical stretch by factor $2$ gives $y=2x^2$. A translation of $\binom{3}{-1}$ means shift $3$ units right and $1$ unit down, giving $y=2(x-3)^2-1$.

questions.stem: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of $3x^2-6x+1=0$, find $\alpha\beta-\alpha-\beta$.
How many times does the line $y=2x+1$ intersect the parabola $y=x^2$?
questions.explanation: Set equal: $x^2=2x+1$ becomes $x^2-2x-1=0$. The discriminant is $\Delta=(-2)^2-4(1)(-1)=8>0$, so the line cuts the parabola at two distinct points.
